identifiers.title: Alternate day fasting for weight loss in normal weight and overweight subjects: a randomized controlled trial
identifiers.authors: Varady KA, Bhutani S, Klempel MC, Kroeger CM, Trepanowski JF, Haus JM, Hoddy KK, Calvo Y
identifiers.citation: Varady KA, Bhutani S, Klempel MC, Kroeger CM, Trepanowski JF, Haus JM, Hoddy KK, Calvo Y. Alternate day fasting for weight loss in normal weight and overweight subjects: a randomized controlled trial. Nutr J. 2013;12:146. doi:10.1186/1475-2891-12-146

design.quote: A 12-week, randomized, controlled, parallel-arm feeding trial was implemented as a means of testing the study objectives. Subjects were randomized by KAV by way of a stratified random sample. Subjects were first divided into strata based on sex (M/F), age (35–50 y/51-65 y), and BMI (20–24.9 kg/m2/ 25–29.9 kg/m2), and then subjects from each stratum were randomized 1:1 into either the ADF or control group (Figure 1).

species.quote: The experimental protocol was approved by the University of Illinois, Chicago, Office for the Protection of Research Subjects, and all research participants gave their written informed consent to participate in the trial.

population.value: normal weight and overweight adults aged 35–65
population.quote: Inclusion criteria were as follows: BMI between 20 and 29.9 kg/m2; age between 35 and 65 years; pre-menopausal or post-menopausal (absence of menses for more than 2 years); lightly active (< 3 h/week of light intensity exercise at 2.5 to 4.0 metabolic equivalents (METs) for 3 months prior to the study); weight stable for 3 months prior to the beginning of the study (< 4 kg weight loss or weight gain); non-diabetic; no history of cardiovascular disease; non-smoker; and not taking weight loss, lipid- or glucose-lowering medications.

sampleSize.quote: Thirty-two subjects commenced the study, with 30 completing the entire 12-week trial (Figure 1). After loss due to dropouts, the remaining subjects in each intervention group were as follows: ADF (n = 15) and control (n = 15).

facts.label: Fast day: 25% of energy needs, for 24 hours
facts.value: consumed 25% of their baseline energy needs on the fast day (24 h)
facts.quote: During the dietary intervention period, ADF subjects consumed 25% of their baseline energy needs on the fast day (24 h), and then ate ad libitum on each alternating feed day (24 h).

facts.label: Feed day: ate freely
facts.value: ate ad libitum on each alternating feed day
facts.quote: During the dietary intervention period, ADF subjects consumed 25% of their baseline energy needs on the fast day (24 h), and then ate ad libitum on each alternating feed day (24 h).

facts.label: Energy needs worked out with a standard equation (Mifflin)
facts.value: Mifflin equation
facts.quote: Energy needs for each subject were determined by the Mifflin equation [].

facts.label: Fast-day meal eaten between 12:00 and 14:00
facts.value: between 12.00 pm and 2.00 pm
facts.quote: The feed and fast days began at midnight each day, and all fast day meals were consumed between 12.00 pm and 2.00 pm to ensure that each subject was undergoing the same duration of fasting. ADF subjects were provided with meals on each fast day (ranging from 400–600 kcal), and ate ad libitum at home on the feed day.

facts.label: Fast-day meals of 400 to 600 kcal, provided
facts.value: ranging from 400–600 kcal
facts.quote: The feed and fast days began at midnight each day, and all fast day meals were consumed between 12.00 pm and 2.00 pm to ensure that each subject was undergoing the same duration of fasting. ADF subjects were provided with meals on each fast day (ranging from 400–600 kcal), and ate ad libitum at home on the feed day.

facts.label: Fast-day meals followed heart-association guidelines: 30% fat, 15% protein, 55% carbohydrate
facts.value: 30% kcal from fat, 15% kcal from protein, 55% kcal from carbohydrate
facts.quote: Fast day meals were provided as a 3-day rotating menu, and were formulated based on the American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines (30% kcal from fat, 15% kcal from protein, 55% kcal from carbohydrate) [].

facts.label: Allowed on fast days: energy-free drinks, tea, coffee, sugar-free gum, plenty of water
facts.value: energy-free beverages, tea, coffee, and sugar-free gum
facts.quote: ADF subjects were permitted to consume energy-free beverages, tea, coffee, and sugar-free gum, and were encouraged to drink plenty of water.

facts.label: Control group ate freely every day, with no meals provided
facts.value: Control subjects were permitted to eat ad libitum every day
facts.quote: Control subjects were permitted to eat ad libitum every day, and were not provided with meals from the research center.

facts.label: Weighed every week on a beam scale
facts.value: at the beginning of every week
facts.quote: Body weight was assessed to the nearest 0.25 kg at the beginning of every week without shoes and in light clothing using a balance beam scale at the HNRU (HealthOMeter, Sunbeam Products, Boca Raton, FL).

facts.label: Fat and lean mass measured by a body scan (DXA)
facts.value: dual x-ray absorptiometry (DXA)
facts.quote: Body composition (fat mass and fat free mass) was measured using dual x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) (Hologic QDR 4500 W, Hologic Inc., Waltham, MA).

facts.label: Food eaten on feed days came from 3-day food records
facts.value: complete a 3-day food record
facts.quote: To assess energy intake on the feed days, ADF and control subjects were asked to complete a 3-day food record on 2 feed days during the week, and on 1 feed day during the weekend, at week 1 and 12.

facts.label: Extra fast-day food was self-reported in a log
facts.value: report any extra food items consumed
facts.quote: To assess energy intake on the fast days, ADF subjects were asked to report any extra food items consumed (i.e. those not provided) using an “Extra food log”.

facts.label: Results are given as mean ± standard error, not standard deviation
facts.value: means ± standard error of the mean (SEM)
facts.quote: Results are presented as means ± standard error of the mean (SEM).

facts.label: Sample size was planned to detect a 10% change in LDL cholesterol
facts.value: Sample size was calculated assuming a 10% change in LDL-cholesterol concentrations in the ADF group
facts.quote: Sample size was calculated assuming a 10% change in LDL-cholesterol concentrations in the ADF group, with a power of 80% and an alpha risk of 5%.

facts.label: Between-group differences tested with t-tests
facts.value: Between-group differences were tested by an independent samples t-test
facts.quote: Between-group differences were tested by an independent samples t-test.

One other subject reported constipation during week 1 and 2 of the trial. The subject was advised to consume more fruits and vegetables on feed days, and the constipation subsided by week 3 of the dietary intervention period.

facts.label: Alternate-day fasting: a fast day at 25% of energy needs, then a day of eating freely
facts.value: a “fast day” where individuals consume 25% of energy needs
facts.quote: Alternate day fasting involves a “fast day” where individuals consume 25% of energy needs, alternated with a “feed day” where subjects eat ad libitum [].

facts.label: Earlier trials, almost all in people with obesity, found 5 to 6% weight loss in 8 to 12 weeks
facts.value: almost all of these studies have been undertaken in obese populations
facts.quote: Only a handful of studies have been performed to test the effects of ADF on body weight and coronary heart disease (CHD) risk reduction, and almost all of these studies have been undertaken in obese populations (BMI 30–39.9 kg/m2) [-]. Results from these initial trials indicate that ADF is effective for weight loss (5-6% reductions in body weight) and visceral fat mass loss (5–7 cm reductions in waist circumference) in 8–12 weeks of treatment [-].

facts.label: Two earlier, short trials in people without obesity disagreed, and had no control group
facts.value: they are limited by their short durations (2–3 weeks) and their lack of a control group
facts.quote: While these trials [,] lay some groundwork, they are limited by their short durations (2–3 weeks) and their lack of a control group.

facts.label: Authors' estimate: about 0.5 kg a week, whatever the starting weight
facts.value: approximately 0.5 kg/week
facts.quote: Thus, ADF may produce a mean rate of weight loss of approximately 0.5 kg/week, independent of the starting weight or BMI class of the subject.

facts.label: Lean mass was kept, as in earlier short trials
facts.value: Fat free mass was also retained after 12 weeks of ADF
facts.quote: Fat free mass was also retained after 12 weeks of ADF in non-obese individuals.

facts.label: Authors: HDL, homocysteine and resistin usually only improve with more than 10% weight loss
facts.value: generally only improved with >10% weight loss
facts.quote: This lack of effect is not surprising as these CHD risk parameters are generally only improved with >10% weight loss [-].

facts.label: Authors: this is a pilot feasibility report
facts.value: the purpose of this paper is to report pilot feasibility findings
facts.quote: It should also be noted that the purpose of this paper is to report pilot feasibility findings.

facts.label: Authors' summary: a moderate 5 to 6 kg in 12 weeks
facts.value: wishing to lose a moderate amount of weight (5–6 kg) within a relatively short period of time (12 weeks)
facts.quote: In summary, these preliminary findings suggest that ADF is a viable weight loss strategy for normal weight and overweight individuals wishing to lose a moderate amount of weight (5–6 kg) within a relatively short period of time (12 weeks).

facts.label: Planned as normal weight against overweight; the groups were merged after the fact
facts.value: This post hoc change should be taken into consideration
facts.quote: First and foremost, it must be acknowledged that this pilot study was originally designed to compare the effects of ADF in normal weight versus overweight individuals on body weight and CHD risk. Due to a low recruitment rate, we were only able to recruit n = 8 subjects into the normal weight group and n = 8 subjects into the overweight group. In view of this, we decided to combine the normal weight and overweight groups into one group to increase sample size. This post hoc change should be taken into consideration when interpreting the findings of this paper.

facts.label: Physical activity was not measured
facts.value: physical activity was not assessed throughout the trial
facts.quote: Secondly, physical activity was not assessed throughout the trial, thus the degree of weight loss associated with increased energy expenditure from exercise is not known.

facts.label: Small groups: 15 each
facts.value: the sample size of each group was small (n = 15)
facts.quote: Thirdly, the sample size of each group was small (n = 15). Thus, this study may not be adequately powered to detect changes in certain CHD risk parameters (e.g. resistin).

facts.label: Food records: people with overweight under-report by about 30%
facts.value: overweight subject underreport food intake by ~30%
facts.quote: Fourthly, this study employed food records to assess dietary intake/adherence. It is well known that overweight subject underreport food intake by ~30% [,]. Thus, our findings for the hyperphagic response on the feed day may be inaccurate.

facts.label: Larger trials are needed before firm conclusions
facts.value: further research implementing larger sample sizes is required before solid conclusion can be reached
facts.quote: These findings suggest that ADF is effective for weight loss and cardio-protection in normal weight and overweight adults, though further research implementing larger sample sizes is required before solid conclusion can be reached.

facts.label: Only 12 weeks
facts.value: 12 weeks
facts.quote: Thirty-two subjects (BMI 20–29.9 kg/m2) were randomized to either an ADF group or a control group for 12 weeks.
